The paper introduces a deep learning approach for EM nanostructure design using dimensionality reduction.
Autoencoders are used to reduce the dimensionality of both design and response spaces.
The method transforms a many-to-one problem into a one-to-one problem in the reduced spaces.
Dimensionality reduction enables efficient and accurate modeling of complex nanostructures.
The approach significantly reduces computational complexity compared to traditional methods.
The bottleneck layer in the autoencoder represents the reduced space.
The mean-squared error (MSE) is used as the cost function for autoencoder training.
The inverse problem is solved by inverting the one-to-one relation between reduced design and response spaces.
The method is demonstrated for designing reconfigurable metasurfaces based on phase-change materials (PCMs).
The metasurface example uses gold (Au) nanoribbons on a thin layer of germanium antimony telluride (GST).
The refractive index of GST changes from 4.5 to 7 in the near-infrared region when transitioning between amorphous and crystalline states.
The experimental results of the fabricated devices match the predictions of the proposed approach.
Design constraints such as fabrication limitations can be imposed in the final step.
The approach provides intuitive understanding of the roles of different design parameters.
The method is applicable to a wide range of EM nanostructure design problems.
The approach can be integrated with full-wave commercial software packages.
The reduced design parameters allow for efficient and practical design solutions.
The method is particularly useful for complex nanostructures with many design parameters.
The approach can handle nonuniqueness in the design problem.
The method is demonstrated for wideband amplitude modulation of near-infrared light.
The approach reduces the need for extensive computational resources.
The method provides a powerful toolkit for analysis, design, and optimization of EM nanostructures.
The approach can be used to solve complex design problems that were previously intractable.
The method is based on a combination of deep learning and dimensionality reduction techniques.
The approach is validated through both simulation and experimental results.
